addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- amazon-bedrock: Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation (Converse API, InvokeModel), RAG with Knowledge Bases, Bedrock Agents, Guardrails, and AgentCore. Use when invoking models, setting up Knowledge Bases, creating agents, applying guardrails, deploying to AgentCore, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing models (Claude, Llama, [infra], Titan). ALSO USE for prompt caching setup and debugging, quota health checks and throttling diagnosis, cost attribution and tracking, migrating between Claude model generations (4.5 to 4.6 to 4.7), chunking strategies, API selection (Converse vs InvokeModel), guardrail capabilities, and model selection. Also covers AgentCore Payments setup (x402, microtransactions, Payment Manager, Connector, Instrument, Coinbase CDP, Stripe Privy, 402 Payment Required, pay for content, paid endpoint, agent payments). NOT for custom model training, Rekognition, or Comprehend.
- aws-billing-and-cost-management: Analyze AWS costs, find savings, manage budgets, evaluate Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, right-size EC2/Lambda/RDS/EBS with Compute Optimizer, look up service pricing, query CUR with Athena, detect cost anomalies, scope costs to billing views, and monitor Free Tier usage. Triggers on: AWS bill, cost analysis, reduce spend, savings plan, reserved instance, right-size, budget alert, cost optimization, pricing, free tier, cost anomaly, CUR, cost audit, billing view, billing view ARN.
- aws-blocks: Guides building full-stack applications with AWS Blocks — an Infrastructure-from-Code framework. Applies when creating APIs, selecting Building Blocks (KVStore, DistributedTable, Database, AuthBasic, AuthCognito, Realtime, AsyncJob, FileBucket, etc.), running local development, or deploying AWS Blocks applications. Also covers AWS Blocks topics with validated, version-specific patterns that prevent common mistakes. Triggers when user mentions AWS Blocks; project has aws-blocks/ directory; code imports @aws-blocks packages.
- aws-cdk: Authors, deploys, and troubleshoots AWS infrastructure using CDK with TypeScript or Python. Covers best practices, stack architecture, and construct patterns. Always use when writing CDK constructs, bootstrapping environments, running cdk deploy/synth/diff, fixing CDK or CloudFormation errors, planning stack structure, importing existing resources, resolving drift, or refactoring stacks without resource replacement.
- aws-cloudformation: Author, validate, and troubleshoot AWS CloudFormation templates. Covers template authoring with secure defaults, pre-deployment validation (cfn-lint, cfn-guard, change sets), and root-cause diagnosis of failed stacks using CloudFormation events and CloudTrail correlation.
- aws-containers: Deploys and operates containerized workloads on ECS, Fargate, and ECR. Covers task definitions, Fargate services, ECR repository setup and lifecycle policies, ECS Exec debugging, service scaling, deployment strategies, load balancer integration, and logging configuration. Use when deploying, debugging, or optimizing containers on AWS. ALSO USE for container deployment options (ECS vs ECS Express Mode), networking modes, health check troubleshooting, OOM errors, secrets injection, blue/green deployments, ECR image management, and App Runner sunset guidance and migration. NOT for Kubernetes, EKS, or CI/CD pipelines.
- aws-messaging-and-streaming: Guides use of AWS messaging and streaming services. Covers Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon MQ, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK). Use when implementing messaging and streaming patterns.
- aws-observability: Builds, configures, debugs, and optimizes AWS observability with CloudWatch (Log Insights, Metrics, Alarms, Dashboards, EMF), X-Ray, CloudTrail, and ADOT (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), AND enables/onboards services to Application Signals using ADOT auto-instrumentation SDKs. Covers Log Insights queries, alarms (metric, composite, anomaly), dashboards, custom metrics/EMF, X-Ray tracing and sampling, ADOT collector config, CloudTrail auditing, and end-to-end Application Signals enablement via ADOT SDKs (CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, CloudWatch Agent IAM, OTLP endpoints, ServiceEvents, Dynamic Instrumentation), breakpoint and snapshot in Dynamic Instrumentation, live data capture in running service, debug without redeploying. Applies to CloudWatch, alarms, dashboards, EMF, X-Ray, traces, CloudTrail,  ADOT, monitoring, synthetics/canaries, OR enabling/onboarding/instrumenting a service for Application Signals. Not for app logging or security threat detection.
- aws-sdk-js-v3-usage: AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 development patterns. Use when writing JavaScript or TypeScript code that uses AWS services via @aws-sdk/* packages (aws-sdk-js-v3), or when asked about schemas, runtime validation, serialization, or code generation in the context of the JS/TS AWS SDK.
- aws-sdk-python-usage: AWS SDK for Python (boto3/botocore) development patterns. You MUST use this skill when writing Python code that uses AWS services via boto3 or botocore. This includes creating service clients or resources, configuring sessions and credentials, handling errors with ClientError, using paginators and waiters, S3 file transfers and presigned URLs, DynamoDB table operations, and any boto3/botocore client configuration. Use this skill whenever Python code imports boto3 or botocore, or when the user asks about AWS operations in Python.
- aws-sdk-swift-usage: AWS SDK for Swift development patterns. Use when writing Swift code that uses AWS services via aws-sdk-swift package.
- aws-serverless: Builds, deploys, manages, debugs, configures, and optimizes serverless applications on AWS using Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, EventBridge, and SAM/CDK. Covers cold starts, CORS debugging, event source mappings, troubleshooting, concurrency, SnapStart, Powertools, function URLs, EventBridge Scheduler, Lambda layers, and production readiness. Triggers on mentions of Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, SAM templates, CDK serverless stacks, DynamoDB stream triggers, SQS event sources, cold starts, timeouts, 502/504 errors, throttling, concurrency, CORS, Powertools, or any event-driven architecture on AWS, even without the word "serverless." Does not apply to EC2, ECS/Fargate containers, or Amplify hosting.
- cso: Chief Security Officer mode. (gstack)
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- investigate: Systematic debugging with root cause investigation. (gstack)
- office-hours: YC Office Hours — two modes. (gstack)
- review: Pre-landing PR review. (gstack)
- signing-in-to-aws: Gets AWS credentials for CLI/SDK access via `aws login`. Activates when a developer needs to authenticate to AWS for local development, when an AWS operation fails due to missing or expired credentials, or when someone asks about setting up AWS access. Triggers: "set up AWS", "configure AWS", "aws login", "get credentials", "authenticate", "session expired", "token expired", "no credentials", "AccessDeniedException" with no configured credentials.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	---
2	redu_schema: 2
3	repo: https://github.com/bewcloud/bewcloud
4	plan:
5	  tool: deploy_compose
6	  image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
7	  port: 8000
8	  vm: m1.medium
9	  flavor_id: "3"
10	  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
11	  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
12	bootstrap:
13	  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
14	  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
15	  source: bewcloud
16	quirks:
17	  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: THE FIRST PERSON TO SUBMIT THE SIGNUP FORM, AND THE SETTING THAT LOOKS LIKE IT PREVENTS THIS DOES NOT. Upstream says it in the README in an IMPORTANT block (README.md:44-46): even with signups disabled, the first signup will work and become an admin. The code says it twice. lib/config.ts:123-136 returns 'signup allowed' whenever no admin exists, whatever allowSignups is set to, and lib/models/user.ts:65-69 flags that first account is_admin and dates its subscription to the year 2100. So the window opens the moment redu's hostname resolves and closes ONLY when an account exists. No configuration file closes it. CLAIM THE ACCOUNT AS PART OF THE DEPLOY, before you hand the URL to anyone, using the script in this document, and then let the script prove that a second anonymous signup is refused. Never leave a fresh bewCloud sitting on a public hostname."
18	  - "⛔ WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH BEFORE ANYONE SIGNS IN, from routes.ts:181-196,198,272-275,286-291: / (a 303 to /login), /login, /signup, /robots.txt, /favicon.ico, the static assets under /public/*, and the /file-share/* trio. The file-share routes only serve anything once a logged-in user has explicitly created a share AND config.files.allowPublicSharing is true, which defaults to FALSE (lib/config.ts:26) and which this recipe leaves false. /caldav and /carddav answer 401 with a Basic challenge to anyone without a session (pages/caldav.ts:12-17). Everything else, files, notes, photos, contacts, calendar and expenses, requires a session cookie. So the whole exposure is the signup form, and the quirk above is how you close it."
19	  - "⛔ AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT, allowSignups: false IS WHAT KEEPS IT CLOSED, and it is already the default in both the sample config and the built-in defaults (bewcloud.config.sample.ts:7, lib/config.ts:13). Leave it false unless the user actually wants an open instance. If they do want extra accounts, the honest options are to flip it to true for a few minutes and back, or to run with enableSingleSignOn and allowSignupsViaSingleSignOn against their own identity provider. Note allowSignupsViaSingleSignOn OVERRIDES allowSignups for the SSO path specifically (lib/config.ts:126-128); do not set it and assume the front door is still shut."
20	  - "⛔⛔ THE DATABASE FAILS OPEN TO A MOCK, NOT TO SQLITE, AND THIS IS THE ONE THAT WOULD BREAK THE DEPLOY WITHOUT ANYTHING GOING RED. lib/interfaces/database.ts:70-87: if the Postgres connection throws, bewCloud logs 'Failed to connect to Postgres!' once and then installs a stub client whose every query returns an empty row set, under the comment that this lets the app work even when Postgres is not available. The container stays up, the hostname serves, /login renders, and every account, file record and note silently does not exist. A health check on / passes perfectly. The compose in this document defends against that by running migrate-db as a one-shot service that the app DEPENDS ON: migrate-db.ts:9 builds its Database with throwOnConnectionError true and exits 1 on failure, so a bad database stops the app from starting at all instead of letting it serve a hollow site."
21	  - "⛔ MIGRATIONS DO NOT RUN AT APP BOOT. THERE IS NO AUTO-MIGRATE. Upstream's install is two commands, not one (README.md:31-33): bring the stack up, THEN run 'docker compose run --rm website bash -c \"cd /app && make migrate-db\"'. Skip it and there are no tables; combined with the mock-client fallback above, the site looks fine and stores nothing. The compose in this document folds it in as a migrate-db service so it cannot be forgotten, and the runner is idempotent: it records executed files in bewcloud_migrations and prints 'No migrations to run!' on every later boot (migrate-db.ts:66-101)."
22	  - "⛔ PROVE THE DATABASE WIRING IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, BECAUSE AN ABSENCE ALONE PROVES NOTHING. Positive half, which is also what tells you your command ran at all: 'sudo docker compose logs migrate-db | grep -cE \"Success!|No migrations to run!\"' must be at least 1. Negative half: 'sudo docker compose logs website | grep -c \"Failed to connect to Postgres!\"' must be 0. If the first command errors or returns 0, the second one's zero means nothing at all. Then confirm the real thing: 'sudo docker exec <website container> printenv POSTGRESQL_HOST POSTGRESQL_DBNAME' must name the private database VM. The VM runs docker, not podman, and containers are named after the compose project redu unpacks into, so find the name with 'sudo docker ps' rather than guessing it."
23	  - "⛔ NAME MAPPING: bewCloud DOES NOT READ redu's injected variables. redu appends PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD, PGDATABASE and DATABASE_URL to the project .env; bewCloud reads POSTGRESQL_HOST, POSTGRESQL_PORT, POSTGRESQL_USER, POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD and POSTGRESQL_DBNAME (lib/interfaces/database.ts:4-9) and understands no connection URL at all. deploy_compose only APPENDS to the .env, it never edits your compose, so the compose must do the mapping itself with ${PGHOST} and friends. The compose in this document does exactly that. Get one name wrong and you get the silent mock client, not an error."
24	  - "⛔⛔ TWO SECRETS THAT A REDEPLOY DESTROYS, BOTH DEFAULTING TO THE EMPTY STRING WITH NO WARNING (lib/auth.ts:10-11). PASSWORD_SALT is mixed into every stored password: [REDACTED:value] hash is SHA-256 of '<password>:<PASSWORD_SALT>' (pages/signup.ts:85). CHANGE IT AND EVERY ACCOUNT ON THE INSTANCE IS LOCKED OUT PERMANENTLY, including the admin, and with no SMTP configured there is no password-reset path back in. JWT_SECRET signs the session cookie and the API tokens; change it and everyone is logged out. Generate both once, as long alphanumeric strings, store them where the user keeps their secrets, and pass the SAME values on every redeploy. Leaving them empty is not an error and not a warning; it is just a weaker hash that you must then keep empty forever."
25	  - "⛔ CONFIGURATION IS A TYPESCRIPT FILE, NOT ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES, AND THE BIND MOUNT IS A FILE MOUNT. Since v2 the .env holds secrets only and bewcloud.config.ts holds configuration (FAQ.md:23). The BEWCLOUD_AUTH_* and BEWCLOUD_FILES_* variables you will find in tutorials and in the FAQ itself come from a user's comment on issue #90; they are a hack that needs you to write that config file, and the shipped app reads none of them. The compose bind-mounts ./bewcloud.config.ts onto /app/bewcloud.config.ts, so if that file is missing from your uploaded source Docker helpfully creates a DIRECTORY there, the import fails, and lib/config.ts:111 logs an error and quietly continues on the defaults, which point baseUrl at http://localhost:8000. PROVE IT BOTH WAYS: 'sudo docker compose logs website | grep -c \"Config loaded from bewcloud.config.ts\"' must be at least 1 (the positive half) AND 'grep -c \"Error loading config from bewcloud.config.ts\"' must be 0."
26	  - "⛔ auth.baseUrl MUST BE THE REAL HTTPS HOSTNAME, SET BEFORE THE FIRST BOOT, so generate the dname yourself up front in full bewcloud-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form and write it into bewcloud.config.ts. It defaults to http://localhost:8000 (lib/config.ts:11) and upstream's own comment on that field says authentication will not work without https:// except on localhost (bewcloud.config.sample.ts:6). It also decides the session cookie domain (lib/auth.ts:55-66) and, if you ever enable SSO, the OIDC redirect is this value plus /oidc/callback. A wrong baseUrl presents as 'I can sign up but I cannot stay logged in', which reads like a platform fault."
27	  - "⛔ PUBLISH PORT 8000 ON 0.0.0.0, NOT ON 127.0.0.1. The upstream compose maps '127.0.0.1:8000:8000' (docker-compose.yml:10) because it assumes a reverse proxy running on the same host. redu's TLS terminator is not on your VM, so a loopback binding means the hostname answers 502 forever while the container looks perfectly healthy. Map '8000:8000' and pass port 8000 to deploy_compose. The image exposes 8000 and PORT defaults to it."
28	  - "⛔ NEVER PUBLISH RADICALE'S PORT 5232. Its authentication type is http_x_remote_user (radicale-config/config, [auth]), which means it trusts whatever X-Remote-User header arrives and does no authentication of its own. bewCloud sets that header from the authenticated session and proxies /caldav and /carddav through its own port (pages/caldav.ts:45), which is why the upstream compose leaves Radicale's port mapping commented out (docker-compose.yml:41-42). Expose 5232 and anyone on the internet can read and rewrite any user's calendars and contacts by setting one header. Keep it on the compose network only. Your phone syncs against https://<your-host>/caldav/ and /carddav/, not against 5232."
29	  - "⛔ FILE OWNERSHIP: THE UPLOADS DIRECTORY MUST BE OWNED BY UID 1993 BEFORE THE APP TOUCHES IT. The image runs as the deno user, uid 1993 (Dockerfile:17, and the README documents the number at README.md:36-38), and it declares no VOLUME, so a named Docker volume mounted at /app/data-files is created root-owned and empty and every upload fails with a permission error while the app itself looks healthy. The compose in this document runs a one-shot init-permissions service, as root, from the SAME already-pulled image so there is no second pin, that does mkdir -p and chown -R 1993:1993 on the bind-mounted directory before anything else starts. It is a no-op when ownership is already right. Radicale does NOT need this: its image ships TAKE_FILE_OWNERSHIP=true with BUILD_UID 2999 and is granted cap_add CHOWN for exactly that reason."
30	  - "PERSIST data-files AND data-radicale, AND KNOW WHICH STORE HOLDS WHAT. Postgres holds accounts, sessions, file METADATA, notes, news, expenses and share records. ./data-files holds every actual uploaded byte, and ./data-radicale/collections holds every calendar event and contact card. Lose those directories and the database still lists files that no longer exist. Both must be on the app VM's persistent storage, and both go with the deployment when you delete it."
31	  - "DISK IS THE CONSTRAINT HERE, NOT MEMORY, AND YOU MUST PUT THAT IN FRONT OF THE USER BEFORE SIZING. This is a file-sync product: whatever they put in it lands on the app VM's flavor disk. m1.small gives 20 GB, m1.medium 40 GB, m1.large 80 GB, and growing later is a volume resize rather than a redeploy. This recipe picks m1.medium for the 40 GB, not for the RAM. The default per-file upload cap is 100 MB (lib/config.ts:28, files.maxUploadSizeInMegabytes) and the default request cap is 12 MB (core.maxRequestSizeInMegabytes); neither is a cap on total storage, and nothing stops the disk filling."
32	  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO MEASUREMENT. The only resource figures anywhere in the repo are two mem_limit: '256m' lines in docker-compose.yml, one for the app and one for Radicale, and those are ceilings the author chose rather than observations. Reasoning: a Deno server with its frontend prebuilt into the image, plus a small Python CalDav server, comfortably inside m1.medium's 4 GB. Measure it on your run and write the real figure back, because it is the most useful thing a first deploy can add to this file."
33	  - "ONE DATABASE, NO SUPERUSER, NO EXTENSIONS. Measured across all four files in db-migrations/: 10 CREATE TABLE and 3 CREATE UNIQUE INDEX (the control proving the grep worked) and ZERO CREATE EXTENSION, CREATE DATABASE or CREATE SCHEMA. Primary keys use gen_random_uuid(), which has been built into Postgres since 13, so pgcrypto is not needed. bewCloud therefore never hits redu's one-database-per-managed-Postgres limit, and db_superuser is not required."
34	  - "SSL TO THE DATABASE IS ATTEMPTED AND SILENTLY OPTIONAL. lib/interfaces/database.ts:11-20 builds its TLS options as enabled true, enforce FALSE, so it tries an encrypted connection and continues unencrypted if the server declines. There is no sslmode string to set. POSTGRESQL_CAFILE is the only lever: point it at a CA bundle inside the container and the certificate is verified against it. Over redu's private network the default is survivable; say in the handover which one you left in place rather than staying silent about it."
35	  - "DELETE THE BUNDLED POSTGRES SERVICE FROM THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE. docker-compose.yml:19-35 ships a postgres:18.4 container with a placeholder password, on a local Docker volume. On redu that is a second database nobody manages, nobody backs up and you still pay to run, sitting beside the managed one. The compose in this document has it removed. Keep Radicale; drop Postgres."
36	  - "PIN THE IMAGE. ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0, released 2026-08-13, confirmed present in the registry's own tag list (95 tags). A latest tag exists on ghcr too, so a habit-written :latest will resolve rather than 404, which makes it more dangerous here and not less: this project ships minor versions weekly and a redeploy that crosses one silently changes your app. Radicale is pinned at tomsquest/docker-radicale:[ip], the version upstream's own compose uses."
37	  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> generate the dname yourself and write https://<that>.redu.cloud into bewcloud.config.ts as auth.baseUrl -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr, roughly GBP 33 a month; fits the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2', port 8000. Pass db_flavor_id explicitly: omitting it defaults the database VM to the app flavor and doubles the bill. plan_deploy will want to upsize a compose stack to m1.large, which is the right default for things that BUILD from source and wrong here, since every image is pulled; passing flavor_id '3' holds m1.medium. Then run the claim script in this file BEFORE giving anyone the URL."
38	  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source. Write docker-compose.yml, bewcloud.config.ts, radicale-config/config and an empty data-files directory locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. The config file and the Radicale config file MUST be in that upload: they are bind-mounted by path, and Docker silently substitutes a directory for a missing file mount."
39	  - "LICENCE: AGPL-3.0, and here the third-party metadata happens to be right. The practical difference from GPL is section 13, the network clause: if you MODIFY bewCloud and let other people use it over a network, you owe those users your modified source. Pulling the official image unchanged and running it for yourself and the accounts you create triggers nothing extra. Note that section 13 places that obligation on whoever OPERATES the service, which is the user, not redu."
40	  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. JWT_SECRET, PASSWORD_SALT, the admin password and the database password all belong to the user. Hand them over in the session; the deploy log records that an admin account was claimed and that signup is closed, never the values."
41	  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back. ⚠️ Do not assume that captured what your run learned: when this file is richer than redu's template the merge returns redu_md_merge_mode 'in_place', which refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and NOTHING ELSE. Any new quirk you found has to be added by hand."
42	  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but keeps the managed Postgres, so accounts and file metadata survive, and that database keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. ⚠️ THE ACTUAL FILES DO NOT SURVIVE: data-files and data-radicale live on the app VM, so every uploaded byte, every calendar event and every contact goes with the deployment while the rows describing them remain. Say that plainly before deleting, and use delete_database when the user really means all of it."
43	---
44	
45	# Self-host bewCloud on redu
46	
47	A simpler alternative to Nextcloud and ownCloud: files, notes, photos, expenses, contacts and
48	calendar, on one small VM in the EU, on your own hostname with TLS. One Deno container, a
49	CalDav/CardDav sidecar it proxies for you, and a managed Postgres beside them.
50	
51	## What this deploys
52	
53	- **bewCloud** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM, port 8000.
54	- **Radicale**, the CalDav/CardDav server, on the compose network only. bewCloud proxies it at
55	  `/caldav/` and `/carddav/`, so your phone syncs over the same HTTPS hostname.
56	- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so accounts and file metadata survive every redeploy.
57	- Persistent directories for uploaded files and for calendars and contacts.
58	- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.
59	
60	About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.
61	
62	**Size for disk, not memory.** This is a file-sync app, so whatever you put in it lands on the VM's
63	flavor disk: 20 GB on m1.small, 40 GB on m1.medium, 80 GB on m1.large. Growing it later is a volume
64	resize rather than a redeploy, so pick before you deploy. This recipe defaults to m1.medium for the
65	40 GB.
66	
67	## Deploy
68	
69	Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
70	directory containing this file:
71	
72	    Read redu.md and deploy bewCloud on redu.
73	
74	The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.
75	
76	## The compose
77	
78	Upstream's `docker-compose.yml` is a real deploy, unusually, so this is that file with three
79	changes: its bundled `postgres:18.4` removed in favour of the managed database, its loopback port
80	binding opened up because redu's TLS terminator is not on your VM, and two one-shot services added
81	so that neither the file permissions nor the migrations can be forgotten.
82	
83	```yaml
84	services:
85	  # Runs as root, from the SAME image, so there is no second pin. Fixes the upload directory's
86	  # ownership to uid 1993 (the deno user) before anything else starts. No-op if already correct.
87	  init-permissions:
88	    image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
89	    user: "0:0"
90	    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
91	    command: ["mkdir -p /app/data-files && chown -R 1993:1993 /app/data-files"]
92	    restart: "no"
93	    volumes:
94	      - ./data-files:/app/data-files
95	
96	  # Exits non-zero if the database is wrong, which stops the app starting rather than letting it
97	  # serve a hollow site off the mock client. Idempotent on every later boot.
98	  migrate-db:
99	    image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
100	    command: ["task", "migrate-db"]
101	    restart: "no"
102	    depends_on:
103	      init-permissions:
104	        condition: service_completed_successfully
105	    environment:
106	      POSTGRESQL_HOST: "${PGHOST}"
107	      POSTGRESQL_PORT: "${PGPORT}"
108	      POSTGRESQL_USER: "${PGUSER}"
109	      POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
110	      POSTGRESQL_DBNAME: "${PGDATABASE}"
111	
112	  website:
113	    image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
114	    restart: always
115	    depends_on:
116	      migrate-db:
117	        condition: service_completed_successfully
118	    ports:
119	      - "8000:8000"
120	    mem_limit: "512m"
121	    environment:
122	      PORT: "8000"
123	      POSTGRESQL_HOST: "${PGHOST}"
124	      POSTGRESQL_PORT: "${PGPORT}"
125	      POSTGRESQL_USER: "${PGUSER}"
126	      POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
127	      POSTGRESQL_DBNAME: "${PGDATABASE}"
128	      JWT_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
129	      PASSWORD_SALT: "[REDACTED:value]}"
130	    volumes:
131	      - ./data-files:/app/data-files
132	      - ./bewcloud.config.ts:/app/bewcloud.config.ts
133	
134	  # No published port, deliberately. See the quirk about X-Remote-User.
135	  radicale:
136	    image: tomsquest/docker-radicale:[ip]
137	    init: true
138	    read_only: true
139	    restart: always
140	    security_opt:
141	      - no-new-privileges:true
142	    cap_drop:
143	      - ALL
144	    cap_add:
145	      - SETUID
146	      - SETGID
147	      - CHOWN
148	      - KILL
149	    mem_limit: "256m"
150	    volumes:
151	      - ./data-radicale:/data
152	      - ./radicale-config:/config:ro
153	```
154	
155	`PGHOST` and the rest are injected by redu. `JWT_SECRET` and `PASSWORD_SALT` are yours to
156	generate, once, and to keep.
157	
158	And `bewcloud.config.ts`, which must be in the upload because it is bind-mounted by path:
159	
160	```ts
161	import { Config, PartialDeep } from './lib/types.ts';
162	
163	const config: PartialDeep<Config> = {
164	  auth: {
165	    baseUrl: 'https://bewcloud-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud', // the dname you generated, in full
166	    allowSignups: false,
167	    enableEmailVerification: false,
168	    enableForeverSignup: true,
169	    enableMultiFactor: false,
170	  },
171	  files: {
172	    allowPublicSharing: false,
173	  },
174	};
175	
176	export default config;
177	```
178	
179	## The three that actually break it
180	
181	**The signup race.** Upstream states it in an IMPORTANT block in its own README: *even with signups
182	disabled, the first signup will work and become an admin*. It is enforced in two places in the code
183	and no setting turns it off. From the moment the hostname resolves until somebody claims the
184	account, whoever loads `/signup` first owns the instance and every file in it. Claim it as part of
185	the deploy.
186	
187	**The database fails open to a mock.** bewCloud does not fall back to SQLite; it installs a stub
188	client that answers every query with zero rows and keeps serving. The site renders, the health
189	check passes, and nothing is stored anywhere. The compose above turns that into a loud failure by
190	making the app depend on a migration run that exits non-zero.
191	
192	**Configuration is a TypeScript file, and it is bind-mounted by path.** Miss it out of the upload
193	and Docker creates a directory in its place, the import fails, and the app carries on with
194	`baseUrl: http://localhost:8000`. You can sign up and you cannot stay signed in.
195	
196	## Claim the admin account, then prove signup is closed
197	
198	Run this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you give the URL to anyone.
199	
200	It gates every assertion on proof that bewCloud is what is answering, because redu's hostname
201	returns 502 from its proxy for the first couple of minutes while the container starts, and an error
202	page fails every check that reads "did it NOT do X". It exits `2` for inconclusive rather than
203	passing when it cannot tell.
204	
205	```bash
206	#!/usr/bin/env bash
207	# Claim the first (admin) account on a fresh bewCloud, then prove registration is now refused.
208	#   BEWCLOUD_EMAIL=you@example.com BEWCLOUD_PASSWORD=«REDACTED:assigned:6407e69c» ./claim-admin.sh bewcloud-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
209	# Exit 0 = you own it and signup is closed, 1 = OPEN or already taken (act now), 2 = inconclusive.
210	set -eu
211	HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host>}"
212	: "${BEWCLOUD_EMAIL:?set BEWCLOUD_EMAIL in the environment, not on the command line}"
213	: "${BEWCLOUD_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] BEWCLOUD_PASSWORD (6+ chars, alphanumeric so nothing needs escaping)}"
214	TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
215	
216	# 1. GATE. Without this every assertion below is vacuous.
217	code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/login")
218	if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
219	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /login answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
220	  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Wait and re-run. NOT a pass." >&2
221	  exit 2
222	fi
223	
224	# 2. POSITIVE CONTROL. Every bewCloud page titles itself "<prefix> - bewCloud".
225	if ! grep -q '<title>Login - bewCloud</title>' "$TMP/login"; then
226	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /login returned 200 but does not identify as bewCloud." >&2
227	  exit 2
228	fi
229	echo "OK: bewCloud is serving on https://$HOST"
230	
231	# 3. CLAIM IT. Body on stdin via a file, never in argv, where ps would show it.
232	printf 'email=%s&password=[REDACTED:value]' "$BEWCLOUD_EMAIL" "$BEWCLOUD_PASSWORD" > "$TMP/body"
233	code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/signup" -D "$TMP/hdr" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
234	  -H 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-binary @"$TMP/body" \
235	  "https://$HOST/signup")
236	case "$code" in
237	  303)
238	    grep -qi 'success=signup' "$TMP/hdr" || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 303 to an unexpected place." >&2; exit 2; }
239	    echo "OK: admin account created for $BEWCLOUD_EMAIL"
240	    ;;
241	  200)
242	    if grep -q 'Signups are not allowed' "$TMP/signup"; then
243	      echo "FAIL: signup is already refused, which means AN ACCOUNT ALREADY EXISTS." >&2
244	      echo "  If you did not create it, someone else holds the admin seat on this instance." >&2
245	      echo "  Do not put data in it. Destroy the deployment and redeploy." >&2
246	      exit 1
247	    fi
248	    if grep -q 'Email is already in use' "$TMP/signup"; then
249	      echo "OK: that address already has an account here (you have run this before)."
250	    else
251	      echo "INCONCLUSIVE: signup returned 200 with an error this script does not recognise." >&2
252	      exit 2
253	    fi
254	    ;;
255	  *)
256	    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: signup answered HTTP $code." >&2
257	    exit 2
258	    ;;
259	esac
260	
261	# 4. PROVE THE OUTCOME, NOT THE STATUS CODE. A created account is not the same as a usable one.
262	printf 'email=%s&password=[REDACTED:value]' "$BEWCLOUD_EMAIL" "$BEWCLOUD_PASSWORD" > "$TMP/body"
263	code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -D "$TMP/lhdr" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
264	  -H 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-binary @"$TMP/body" \
265	  "https://$HOST/login")
266	if [ "$code" != "303" ] || ! grep -qi 'set-cookie: *bewcloud-app-v1=' "$TMP/lhdr"; then
267	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the account exists but signing in did not return a session (HTTP $code)." >&2
268	  echo "  The usual cause is auth.baseUrl in bewcloud.config.ts not matching this hostname." >&2
269	  exit 2
270	fi
271	echo "OK: signed in, session cookie issued."
272	
273	# 5. THE ASSERTION, on behaviour rather than on a config value.
274	probe="probe$(date +%s)@example.com"
275	printf 'email=%s&password=[REDACTED:value]' "$probe" "notarealpassword" > "$TMP/body"
276	code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/probe" -D "$TMP/phdr" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
277	  -H 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-binary @"$TMP/body" \
278	  "https://$HOST/signup")
279	if [ "$code" = "303" ] && grep -qi 'success=signup' "$TMP/phdr"; then
280	  echo "FAIL: registration is OPEN. An anonymous stranger just created $probe on your VM." >&2
281	  echo "  Set allowSignups: false in bewcloud.config.ts, redeploy, and delete that account." >&2
282	  exit 1
283	fi
284	if grep -q 'Signups are not allowed' "$TMP/probe"; then
285	  echo "OK: a second anonymous signup is refused. You own this instance."
286	  exit 0
287	fi
288	echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the probe signup answered HTTP $code with an unfamiliar body." >&2
289	echo "  Do not leave the instance unattended on the strength of this. Check it by hand." >&2
290	exit 2
291	```
292	
293	## Licence, since it is a fair question
294	
295	bewCloud is **AGPL-3.0**. The practical difference from GPL is section 13, the network clause:
296	modify it and let other people use your modified version over a network, and you owe those users
297	your source. Pulling the official image unchanged and running it for yourself and the accounts you
298	create does not trigger anything. That obligation, when it applies, is on whoever operates the
299	service, which is you and not redu.
300	
301	## Deploy log
302	
303	- Not yet deployed. The first real run replaces this line with its measured time, flavor and hourly
304	  rate, and corrects anything above that turned out to be wrong. The most useful things it can add
305	  are a memory figure and the actual free disk after install, because upstream publishes neither.
306

---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/bewcloud/bewcloud
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
  port: 8000
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: bewcloud
quirks:
  - "⛔⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR, AND WHEN: THE FIRST PERSON TO SUBMIT THE SIGNUP FORM, AND THE SETTING THAT LOOKS LIKE IT PREVENTS THIS DOES NOT. Upstream says it in the README in an IMPORTANT block (README.md:44-46): even with signups disabled, the first signup will work and become an admin. The code says it twice. lib/config.ts:123-136 returns 'signup allowed' whenever no admin exists, whatever allowSignups is set to, and lib/models/user.ts:65-69 flags that first account is_admin and dates its subscription to the year 2100. So the window opens the moment redu's hostname resolves and closes ONLY when an account exists. No configuration file closes it. CLAIM THE ACCOUNT AS PART OF THE DEPLOY, before you hand the URL to anyone, using the script in this document, and then let the script prove that a second anonymous signup is refused. Never leave a fresh bewCloud sitting on a public hostname."
  - "⛔ WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST CAN REACH BEFORE ANYONE SIGNS IN, from routes.ts:181-196,198,272-275,286-291: / (a 303 to /login), /login, /signup, /robots.txt, /favicon.ico, the static assets under /public/*, and the /file-share/* trio. The file-share routes only serve anything once a logged-in user has explicitly created a share AND config.files.allowPublicSharing is true, which defaults to FALSE (lib/config.ts:26) and which this recipe leaves false. /caldav and /carddav answer 401 with a Basic challenge to anyone without a session (pages/caldav.ts:12-17). Everything else, files, notes, photos, contacts, calendar and expenses, requires a session cookie. So the whole exposure is the signup form, and the quirk above is how you close it."
  - "⛔ AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT, allowSignups: false IS WHAT KEEPS IT CLOSED, and it is already the default in both the sample config and the built-in defaults (bewcloud.config.sample.ts:7, lib/config.ts:13). Leave it false unless the user actually wants an open instance. If they do want extra accounts, the honest options are to flip it to true for a few minutes and back, or to run with enableSingleSignOn and allowSignupsViaSingleSignOn against their own identity provider. Note allowSignupsViaSingleSignOn OVERRIDES allowSignups for the SSO path specifically (lib/config.ts:126-128); do not set it and assume the front door is still shut."
  - "⛔⛔ THE DATABASE FAILS OPEN TO A MOCK, NOT TO SQLITE, AND THIS IS THE ONE THAT WOULD BREAK THE DEPLOY WITHOUT ANYTHING GOING RED. lib/interfaces/database.ts:70-87: if the Postgres connection throws, bewCloud logs 'Failed to connect to Postgres!' once and then installs a stub client whose every query returns an empty row set, under the comment that this lets the app work even when Postgres is not available. The container stays up, the hostname serves, /login renders, and every account, file record and note silently does not exist. A health check on / passes perfectly. The compose in this document defends against that by running migrate-db as a one-shot service that the app DEPENDS ON: migrate-db.ts:9 builds its Database with throwOnConnectionError true and exits 1 on failure, so a bad database stops the app from starting at all instead of letting it serve a hollow site."
  - "⛔ MIGRATIONS DO NOT RUN AT APP BOOT. THERE IS NO AUTO-MIGRATE. Upstream's install is two commands, not one (README.md:31-33): bring the stack up, THEN run 'docker compose run --rm website bash -c \"cd /app && make migrate-db\"'. Skip it and there are no tables; combined with the mock-client fallback above, the site looks fine and stores nothing. The compose in this document folds it in as a migrate-db service so it cannot be forgotten, and the runner is idempotent: it records executed files in bewcloud_migrations and prints 'No migrations to run!' on every later boot (migrate-db.ts:66-101)."
  - "⛔ PROVE THE DATABASE WIRING IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, BECAUSE AN ABSENCE ALONE PROVES NOTHING. Positive half, which is also what tells you your command ran at all: 'sudo docker compose logs migrate-db | grep -cE \"Success!|No migrations to run!\"' must be at least 1. Negative half: 'sudo docker compose logs website | grep -c \"Failed to connect to Postgres!\"' must be 0. If the first command errors or returns 0, the second one's zero means nothing at all. Then confirm the real thing: 'sudo docker exec <website container> printenv POSTGRESQL_HOST POSTGRESQL_DBNAME' must name the private database VM. The VM runs docker, not podman, and containers are named after the compose project redu unpacks into, so find the name with 'sudo docker ps' rather than guessing it."
  - "⛔ NAME MAPPING: bewCloud DOES NOT READ redu's injected variables. redu appends PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD, PGDATABASE and DATABASE_URL to the project .env; bewCloud reads POSTGRESQL_HOST, POSTGRESQL_PORT, POSTGRESQL_USER, POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD and POSTGRESQL_DBNAME (lib/interfaces/database.ts:4-9) and understands no connection URL at all. deploy_compose only APPENDS to the .env, it never edits your compose, so the compose must do the mapping itself with ${PGHOST} and friends. The compose in this document does exactly that. Get one name wrong and you get the silent mock client, not an error."
  - "⛔⛔ TWO SECRETS THAT A REDEPLOY DESTROYS, BOTH DEFAULTING TO THE EMPTY STRING WITH NO WARNING (lib/auth.ts:10-11). PASSWORD_SALT is mixed into every stored password: [REDACTED:value] hash is SHA-256 of '<password>:<PASSWORD_SALT>' (pages/signup.ts:85). CHANGE IT AND EVERY ACCOUNT ON THE INSTANCE IS LOCKED OUT PERMANENTLY, including the admin, and with no SMTP configured there is no password-reset path back in. JWT_SECRET signs the session cookie and the API tokens; change it and everyone is logged out. Generate both once, as long alphanumeric strings, store them where the user keeps their secrets, and pass the SAME values on every redeploy. Leaving them empty is not an error and not a warning; it is just a weaker hash that you must then keep empty forever."
  - "⛔ CONFIGURATION IS A TYPESCRIPT FILE, NOT ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES, AND THE BIND MOUNT IS A FILE MOUNT. Since v2 the .env holds secrets only and bewcloud.config.ts holds configuration (FAQ.md:23). The BEWCLOUD_AUTH_* and BEWCLOUD_FILES_* variables you will find in tutorials and in the FAQ itself come from a user's comment on issue #90; they are a hack that needs you to write that config file, and the shipped app reads none of them. The compose bind-mounts ./bewcloud.config.ts onto /app/bewcloud.config.ts, so if that file is missing from your uploaded source Docker helpfully creates a DIRECTORY there, the import fails, and lib/config.ts:111 logs an error and quietly continues on the defaults, which point baseUrl at http://localhost:8000. PROVE IT BOTH WAYS: 'sudo docker compose logs website | grep -c \"Config loaded from bewcloud.config.ts\"' must be at least 1 (the positive half) AND 'grep -c \"Error loading config from bewcloud.config.ts\"' must be 0."
  - "⛔ auth.baseUrl MUST BE THE REAL HTTPS HOSTNAME, SET BEFORE THE FIRST BOOT, so generate the dname yourself up front in full bewcloud-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud form and write it into bewcloud.config.ts. It defaults to http://localhost:8000 (lib/config.ts:11) and upstream's own comment on that field says authentication will not work without https:// except on localhost (bewcloud.config.sample.ts:6). It also decides the session cookie domain (lib/auth.ts:55-66) and, if you ever enable SSO, the OIDC redirect is this value plus /oidc/callback. A wrong baseUrl presents as 'I can sign up but I cannot stay logged in', which reads like a platform fault."
  - "⛔ PUBLISH PORT 8000 ON 0.0.0.0, NOT ON 127.0.0.1. The upstream compose maps '127.0.0.1:8000:8000' (docker-compose.yml:10) because it assumes a reverse proxy running on the same host. redu's TLS terminator is not on your VM, so a loopback binding means the hostname answers 502 forever while the container looks perfectly healthy. Map '8000:8000' and pass port 8000 to deploy_compose. The image exposes 8000 and PORT defaults to it."
  - "⛔ NEVER PUBLISH RADICALE'S PORT 5232. Its authentication type is http_x_remote_user (radicale-config/config, [auth]), which means it trusts whatever X-Remote-User header arrives and does no authentication of its own. bewCloud sets that header from the authenticated session and proxies /caldav and /carddav through its own port (pages/caldav.ts:45), which is why the upstream compose leaves Radicale's port mapping commented out (docker-compose.yml:41-42). Expose 5232 and anyone on the internet can read and rewrite any user's calendars and contacts by setting one header. Keep it on the compose network only. Your phone syncs against https://<your-host>/caldav/ and /carddav/, not against 5232."
  - "⛔ FILE OWNERSHIP: THE UPLOADS DIRECTORY MUST BE OWNED BY UID 1993 BEFORE THE APP TOUCHES IT. The image runs as the deno user, uid 1993 (Dockerfile:17, and the README documents the number at README.md:36-38), and it declares no VOLUME, so a named Docker volume mounted at /app/data-files is created root-owned and empty and every upload fails with a permission error while the app itself looks healthy. The compose in this document runs a one-shot init-permissions service, as root, from the SAME already-pulled image so there is no second pin, that does mkdir -p and chown -R 1993:1993 on the bind-mounted directory before anything else starts. It is a no-op when ownership is already right. Radicale does NOT need this: its image ships TAKE_FILE_OWNERSHIP=true with BUILD_UID 2999 and is granted cap_add CHOWN for exactly that reason."

Postgres holds accounts, sessions, file METADATA, notes, news, expenses and share records. ./data-files holds every actual uploaded byte, and ./data-radicale/collections holds every calendar event and contact card. Lose those directories and the database still lists files that no longer exist. Both must be on the app VM's persistent storage, and both go with the deployment when you delete it."

This is a file-sync product: whatever they put in it lands on the app VM's flavor disk. m1.small gives 20 GB, m1.medium 40 GB, m1.large 80 GB, and growing later is a volume resize rather than a redeploy. This recipe picks m1.medium for the 40 GB, not for the RAM. # Self-host bewCloud on redu

A simpler alternative to Nextcloud and ownCloud: files, notes, photos, expenses, contacts and
calendar, on one small VM in the EU, on your own hostname with TLS. One Deno container, a
CalDav/CardDav sidecar it proxies for you, and a managed Postgres beside them.

## What this deploys

- **bewCloud** from the official image, pinned, on one m1.medium VM, port 8000.
- **Radicale**, the CalDav/CardDav server, on the compose network only. bewCloud proxies it at
  `/caldav/` and `/carddav/`, so your phone syncs over the same HTTPS hostname.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so accounts and file metadata survive every redeploy.
- Persistent directories for uploaded files and for calendars and contacts.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour, roughly GBP 33 a month. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

**Size for disk, not memory.** This is a file-sync app, so whatever you put in it lands on the VM's
flavor disk: 20 GB on m1.small, 40 GB on m1.medium, 80 GB on m1.large. Growing it later is a volume
resize rather than a redeploy, so pick before you deploy. This recipe defaults to m1.medium for the
40 GB.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy bewCloud on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The compose

Upstream's `docker-compose.yml` is a real deploy, unusually, so this is that file with three
changes: its bundled `postgres:18.4` removed in favour of the managed database, its loopback port
binding opened up because redu's TLS terminator is not on your VM, and two one-shot services added
so that neither the file permissions nor the migrations can be forgotten.

```yaml
services:
  # Runs as root, from the SAME image, so there is no second pin. Fixes the upload directory's
  # ownership to uid 1993 (the deno user) before anything else starts. No-op if already correct.
  init-permissions:
    image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
    user: "0:0"
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    command: ["mkdir -p /app/data-files && chown -R 1993:1993 /app/data-files"]
    restart: "no"
    volumes:
      - ./data-files:/app/data-files

  # Exits non-zero if the database is wrong, which stops the app starting rather than letting it
  # serve a hollow site off the mock client. Idempotent on every later boot.
  migrate-db:
    image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
    command: ["task", "migrate-db"]
    restart: "no"
    depends_on:
      init-permissions:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    environment:
      POSTGRESQL_HOST: "${PGHOST}"
      POSTGRESQL_PORT: "${PGPORT}"
      POSTGRESQL_USER: "${PGUSER}"
      POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      POSTGRESQL_DBNAME: "${PGDATABASE}"

  website:
    image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
    restart: always
    depends_on:
      migrate-db:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    mem_limit: "512m"
    environment:
      PORT: "8000"
      POSTGRESQL_HOST: "${PGHOST}"
      POSTGRESQL_PORT: "${PGPORT}"
      POSTGRESQL_USER: "${PGUSER}"
      POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      POSTGRESQL_DBNAME: "${PGDATABASE}"
      JWT_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      PASSWORD_SALT: "[REDACTED:value]}"
    volumes:
      - ./data-files:/app/data-files
      - ./bewcloud.config.ts:/app/bewcloud.config.ts

  # No published port, deliberately. See the quirk about X-Remote-User.
  radicale:
    image: tomsquest/docker-radicale:[ip]
    init: true
    read_only: true
    restart: always
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    cap_add:
      - SETUID
      - SETGID
      - CHOWN
      - KILL
    mem_limit: "256m"
    volumes:
      - ./data-radicale:/data
      - ./radicale-config:/config:ro
```

`PGHOST` and the rest are injected by redu. `JWT_SECRET` and `PASSWORD_SALT` are yours to
generate, once, and to keep.

And `bewcloud.config.ts`, which must be in the upload because it is bind-mounted by path:

```ts
import { Config, PartialDeep } from './lib/types.ts';

const config: PartialDeep<Config> = {
  auth: {
    baseUrl: 'https://bewcloud-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud', // the dname you generated, in full
    allowSignups: false,
    enableEmailVerification: false,
    enableForeverSignup: true,
    enableMultiFactor: false,
  },
  files: {
    allowPublicSharing: false,
  },
};

export default config;
```

## The three that actually break it

**The signup race.** Upstream states it in an IMPORTANT block in its own README: *even with signups
disabled, the first signup will work and become an admin*. It is enforced in two places in the code
and no setting turns it off. From the moment the hostname resolves until somebody claims the
account, whoever loads `/signup` first owns the instance and every file in it. Claim it as part of
the deploy.

**The database fails open to a mock.** bewCloud does not fall back to SQLite; it installs a stub
client that answers every query with zero rows and keeps serving. The site renders, the health
check passes, and nothing is stored anywhere. The compose above turns that into a loud failure by
making the app depend on a migration run that exits non-zero.

**Configuration is a TypeScript file, and it is bind-mounted by path.** Miss it out of the upload
and Docker creates a directory in its place, the import fails, and the app carries on with
`baseUrl: http://localhost:8000`. You can sign up and you cannot stay signed in.

## Claim the admin account, then prove signup is closed

Run this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you give the URL to anyone.

It gates every assertion on proof that bewCloud is what is answering, because redu's hostname
returns 502 from its proxy for the first couple of minutes while the container starts, and an error
page fails every check that reads "did it NOT do X". It exits `2` for inconclusive rather than
passing when it cannot tell.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Claim the first (admin) account on a fresh bewCloud, then prove registration is now refused.
#   BEWCLOUD_EMAIL=you@example.com BEWCLOUD_PASSWORD=«REDACTED:assigned:6407e69c» ./claim-admin.sh bewcloud-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
# Exit 0 = you own it and signup is closed, 1 = OPEN or already taken (act now), 2 = inconclusive.
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: claim-admin.sh <host>}"
: "${BEWCLOUD_EMAIL:?set BEWCLOUD_EMAIL in the environment, not on the command line}"
: "${BEWCLOUD_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] BEWCLOUD_PASSWORD (6+ chars, alphanumeric so nothing needs escaping)}"
TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# 1. GATE. Without this every assertion below is vacuous.
code=$(curl -sSL -o "$TMP/login" -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/login")
if [ "$code" != "200" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /login answered HTTP $code, not 200." >&2
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "  502 is redu's proxy while the container starts. Wait and re-run. NOT a pass." >&2
  exit 2
fi

# 2. POSITIVE CONTROL. Every bewCloud page titles itself "<prefix> - bewCloud".
if ! grep -q '<title>Login - bewCloud</title>' "$TMP/login"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /login returned 200 but does not identify as bewCloud." >&2
  exit 2
fi
echo "OK: bewCloud is serving on https://$HOST"

# 3. CLAIM IT. Body on stdin via a file, never in argv, where ps would show it.
printf 'email=%s&password=[REDACTED:value]' "$BEWCLOUD_EMAIL" "$BEWCLOUD_PASSWORD" > "$TMP/body"
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/signup" -D "$TMP/hdr" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
  -H 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-binary @"$TMP/body" \
  "https://$HOST/signup")
case "$code" in
  303)
    grep -qi 'success=signup' "$TMP/hdr" || { echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 303 to an unexpected place." >&2; exit 2; }
    echo "OK: admin account created for $BEWCLOUD_EMAIL"
    ;;
  200)
    if grep -q 'Signups are not allowed' "$TMP/signup"; then
      echo "FAIL: signup is already refused, which means AN ACCOUNT ALREADY EXISTS." >&2
      echo "  If you did not create it, someone else holds the admin seat on this instance." >&2
      echo "  Do not put data in it. Destroy the deployment and redeploy." >&2
      exit 1
    fi
    if grep -q 'Email is already in use' "$TMP/signup"; then
      echo "OK: that address already has an account here (you have run this before)."
    else
      echo "INCONCLUSIVE: signup returned 200 with an error this script does not recognise." >&2
      exit 2
    fi
    ;;
  *)
    echo "INCONCLUSIVE: signup answered HTTP $code." >&2
    exit 2
    ;;
esac

# 4. PROVE THE OUTCOME, NOT THE STATUS CODE. A created account is not the same as a usable one.
printf 'email=%s&password=[REDACTED:value]' "$BEWCLOUD_EMAIL" "$BEWCLOUD_PASSWORD" > "$TMP/body"
code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -D "$TMP/lhdr" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
  -H 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-binary @"$TMP/body" \
  "https://$HOST/login")
if [ "$code" != "303" ] || ! grep -qi 'set-cookie: *bewcloud-app-v1=' "$TMP/lhdr"; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the account exists but signing in did not return a session (HTTP $code)." >&2
  echo "  The usual cause is auth.baseUrl in bewcloud.config.ts not matching this hostname." >&2
  exit 2
fi
echo "OK: signed in, session cookie issued."

# 5. THE ASSERTION, on behaviour rather than on a config value.
probe="probe$(date +%s)@example.com"
printf 'email=%s&password=[REDACTED:value]' "$probe" "notarealpassword" > "$TMP/body"
code=$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/probe" -D "$TMP/phdr" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST \
  -H 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' --data-binary @"$TMP/body" \
  "https://$HOST/signup")
if [ "$code" = "303" ] && grep -qi 'success=signup' "$TMP/phdr"; then
  echo "FAIL: registration is OPEN. An anonymous stranger just created $probe on your VM." >&2
  echo "  Set allowSignups: false in bewcloud.config.ts, redeploy, and delete that account." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if grep -q 'Signups are not allowed' "$TMP/probe"; then
  echo "OK: a second anonymous signup is refused. You own this instance."
  exit 0
fi
echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the probe signup answered HTTP $code with an unfamiliar body." >&2
echo "  Do not leave the instance unattended on the strength of this. Check it by hand." >&2
exit 2
```

## Licence, since it is a fair question

bewCloud is **AGPL-3.0**. The practical difference from GPL is section 13, the network clause:
modify it and let other people use your modified version over a network, and you owe those users
your source. Pulling the official image unchanged and running it for yourself and the accounts you
create does not trigger anything. That obligation, when it applies, is on whoever operates the
service, which is you and not redu.

- Not yet deployed. The first real run replaces this line with its measured time, flavor and hourly
  rate, and corrects anything above that turned out to be wrong. The most useful things it can add
  are a memory figure and the actual free disk after install, because upstream publishes neither.

# CalDAV server hostnames separated by a comma
# IPv4 syntax: address:port
# IPv6 syntax: [address]:port
hosts = 0.0.0.0:5232

# Max parallel connections
#max_connections = 8

# Max size of request body (bytes)
#max_content_length = 100000000

# Socket timeout (seconds)
#timeout = 30


[encoding]

# Encoding for responding requests
#request = utf-8

# Encoding for storing local collections
#stock = utf-8


[auth]

# Authentication method
#type = none
type = http_x_remote_user

# Cache logins for until expiration time
#cache_logins = false

# Expiration time for caching successful logins in seconds
#cache_successful_logins_expiry = 15

## Expiration time of caching failed logins in seconds
#cache_failed_logins_expiry = 90

# IMAP server hostname
# Syntax: address | address:port | [address]:port | imap.server.tld
#imap_host = localhost

# Secure the IMAP connection
# Value: tls | starttls | none
#imap_security = tls

# OAuth2 token endpoint URL
#oauth2_token_endpoint = [REDACTED:value]


[rights]

# Rights backend
# Value: authenticated | owner_only | owner_write | from_file
#type = owner_only

# File for rights management from_file
#file = /etc/radicale/rights

# Permit delete of a collection (global)
#permit_delete_collection = True

# Permit overwrite of a collection (global)
#permit_overwrite_collection = True

# URL Decode the given username (when URL-encoded by the client - useful for iOS devices when using email address)
# urldecode_username = False

[storage]

# Storage backend
# Value: multifilesystem | multifilesystem_nolock
#type = multifilesystem

# Folder for storing local collections, created if not present
filesystem_folder = /data/collections

# Delete sync token that are older (seconds)
#max_sync_token_age = [REDACTED:value]

# Skip broken item instead of triggering an exception
#skip_broken_item = True

[web]

# Web interface backend
# Value: none | internal
#type = internal


[logging]

# Threshold for the logger
# Value: debug | info | warning | error | critical
#level = info

# Don't include passwords in logs
#mask_passwords = True

# Log bad PUT request content
#bad_put_request_content = False

# Log backtrace on level=debug
#backtrace_on_debug = False

# Log request header on level=debug
#request_header_on_debug = False

# Log request content on level=debug
#request_content_on_debug = False

# Log response content on level=debug
#response_content_on_debug = False

# Log rights rule which doesn't match on level=debug
#rights_rule_doesnt_match_on_debug = False

# Log storage cache actions on level=debug
#storage_cache_actions_on_debug = False

[headers]

# Additional HTTP headers
#Access-Control-Allow-Origin = *


[hook]

# Hook types
# Value: none | rabbitmq
#type = none
#rabbitmq_endpoint =
#rabbitmq_topic =
#rabbitmq_queue_type = classic


[reporting]

# When returning a free-busy report, limit the number of returned
# occurences per event to prevent DOS attacks.
#max_freebusy_occurrence = 10000

[HTTP 200]

services:
  website:
    image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
    # NOTE: uncomment below (and comment above) only if you pulled the repo and want to build the image locally
    # build:
    #   context: .
    #   dockerfile: Dockerfile
    restart: always
    ports:
      - 127.0.0.1:8000:8000
    mem_limit: '256m'
    env_file:
      - path: .env
        required: true
    volumes:
      - ./data-files:/app/data-files
      - ./bewcloud.config.ts:/app/bewcloud.config.ts

  postgresql:
    image: postgres:18.4
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_USER=postgres
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value]
      - POSTGRES_DB=bewcloud
    restart: always
    volumes:
      - bewcloud-db:/var/lib/postgresql/18/docker
    # NOTE: uncomment below only if you need to connect to the database from outside the container
    # ports:
    #   - 127.0.0.1:5432:5432
    ulimits:
      memlock:
        soft: -1
        hard: -1
    mem_limit: '256m'

  # NOTE: If you don't want to use the CardDav/CalDav servers, you can comment/remove this service.

    image: tomsquest/docker-radicale:[ip]

    init: true
    read_only: true
    security_opt:

    cap_drop:

    cap_add:

      - SETGID

    volumes:

services:
  # Runs as root, from the SAME image, so there is no second pin. Fixes the upload directory's
  # ownership to uid 1993 (the deno user) before anything else starts. No-op if already correct.
  init-permissions:
    image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
    user: "0:0"
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    command: ["mkdir -p /app/data-files && chown -R 1993:1993 /app/data-files"]
    restart: "no"
    volumes:
      - ./data-files:/app/data-files

  # Exits non-zero if the database is wrong, which stops the app starting rather than letting it
  # serve a hollow site off the mock client. Idempotent on every later boot.
  migrate-db:
    image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
    command: ["task", "migrate-db"]
    restart: "no"
    depends_on:
      init-permissions:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    environment:
      POSTGRESQL_HOST: "${PGHOST}"
      POSTGRESQL_PORT: "${PGPORT}"
      POSTGRESQL_USER: "${PGUSER}"
      POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      POSTGRESQL_DBNAME: "${PGDATABASE}"

  website:
    image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
    restart: always
    depends_on:
      migrate-db:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    mem_limit: "512m"
    environment:
      PORT: "8000"
      POSTGRESQL_HOST: "${PGHOST}"
      POSTGRESQL_PORT: "${PGPORT}"
      POSTGRESQL_USER: "${PGUSER}"
      POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      POSTGRESQL_DBNAME: "${PGDATABASE}"
      JWT_SECRET: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      PASSWORD_SALT: "[REDACTED:value]}"
    volumes:
      - ./data-files:/app/data-files
      - ./bewcloud.config.ts:/app/bewcloud.config.ts

  # No published port, deliberately. Radicale's auth type is http_x_remote_user: it trusts the
  # X-Remote-User header, which bewCloud sets from the authenticated session when it proxies
  # /caldav and /carddav. Publishing 5232 would hand anyone every calendar and contact.
  radicale:
    image: tomsquest/docker-radicale:[ip]
    init: true
    read_only: true
    restart: always
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    cap_add:
      - SETUID
      - SETGID
      - CHOWN
      - KILL
    mem_limit: "256m"
    volumes:
      - ./data-radicale:/data
      - ./radicale-config:/config:ro

---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/bewcloud/bewcloud
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0
  port: 8000
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: bewcloud
quirks:
  - "WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: THE FIRST PERSON TO SUBMIT THE SIGNUP FORM, even with signups disabled (README.md:44-46, lib/config.ts:123-136, lib/models/user.ts:65-69). Claim the account as part of the deploy, before handing the URL to anyone."
  - "THE DATABASE FAILS OPEN TO A MOCK (lib/interfaces/database.ts:70-87). The compose defends against that with migrate-db as a one-shot service the app DEPENDS ON."
  - "MIGRATIONS DO NOT RUN AT APP BOOT. Folded in as a migrate-db service; idempotent."
  - "NAME MAPPING: bewCloud reads POSTGRESQL_* (lib/interfaces/database.ts:4-9), redu injects PG*. The compose maps them itself."
  - "TWO SECRETS A REDEPLOY DESTROYS: PASSWORD_SALT and JWT_SECRET (lib/auth.ts:10-11). Same values on every redeploy."
  - "CONFIGURATION IS A TYPESCRIPT FILE bind-mounted by path; if missing, Docker creates a DIRECTORY and the app falls back to baseUrl http://localhost:8000."
  - "auth.baseUrl MUST BE THE REAL HTTPS HOSTNAME, set before first boot."
  - "PUBLISH PORT 8000 ON 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1: redu's TLS terminator is not on the VM."
  - "NEVER PUBLISH RADICALE'S PORT 5232 (http_x_remote_user auth)."
  - "UPLOADS DIRECTORY MUST BE OWNED BY UID 1993 before the app touches it; init-permissions one-shot does it."
  - "PERSIST data-files AND data-radicale."
  - "DISK IS THE CONSTRAINT, NOT MEMORY: m1.medium for the 40 GB."
  - "ONE DATABASE, NO SUPERUSER, NO EXTENSIONS (10 CREATE TABLE, 0 CREATE EXTENSION)."
  - "DELETE THE BUNDLED POSTGRES SERVICE FROM THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE; keep Radicale."
  - "PIN THE IMAGE: ghcr.io/bewcloud/bewcloud:v4.15.0; radicale tomsquest/docker-radicale:[ip]."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> generate dname -> plan_deploy -> approval -> deploy_compose flavor_id '3', database 'managed', db_engine 'postgres', db_flavor_id '2', port 8000. Pass db_flavor_id explicitly or the DB VM defaults to the app flavor and doubles the bill."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source."
  - "LICENCE: AGPL-3.0."
  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND; data-files and data-radicale do NOT survive."
---

# Self-host bewCloud on redu

A simpler alternative to Nextcloud and ownCloud: files, notes, photos, expenses, contacts and
calendar, on one small VM in the EU, on your own hostname with TLS. One Deno container, a
CalDav/CardDav sidecar it proxies for you, and a managed Postgres beside them.

Deployed with deploy_compose in upload mode, port 8000, m1.medium app VM, managed Postgres on
m1.small. About GBP 0.045/hour.

- NEVER PUBLISH RADICALE'S PORT 5232 (http_x_remote_user auth).
- UPLOADS DIRECTORY MUST BE OWNED BY UID 1993 before the app touches it; init-permissions one-shot does it.

resources.access_point: an auto-generated https://<name>.redu.cloud URL once deployed

warnings: Multi-service compose detected — deploy with deploy_compose (podman-compose on one VM), NOT deploy_app. Pass the EXPOSED service's host port (left side of its `ports:` mapping) + optionally its service name. • The app must start on EVERY boot - a container restart policy or a systemd unit. Never a first-boot-only script. — cloud-init runcmd runs on first boot ONLY. Nothing here builds — every image is pulled — so this deploy passes `flavor_id: "3"` to hold **m1.medium**, exactly as `redu.md` records. m1.medium is chosen for its **40 GB disk**, not its RAM: bewCloud is a file-sync app and every uploaded byte lands on the app VM's flavor disk. Growing later is a volume resize, not a redeploy. ## What gets deployed ```mermaid flowchart LR user([User]) -->|https| ap["Access point
bewcloud-c94m48oq.redu.cloud"] ap --> app subgraph net["your private network"] subgraph vm["App VM — m1.medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB / 40 GB)"] app["website (bewCloud v4.15.0)
host port 8000"] rad["radicale [ip]
CalDav/CardDav — NO published port"] app -->|"proxied /caldav /carddav
X-Remote-User"| rad end pg[("Managed Postgres
m1.small — 1 vCPU / 2 GB / 20 GB")] end app -->|"5432 (private only)"| pg ``` Two one-shot services run before the app and gate it: - `init-permissions` — chowns `./data-files` to uid 1993 (the deno user) so uploads can be written. - `migrate-db` — runs the migrations and **exits non-zero if the database is wrong**, which stops the app starting rather than letting it serve a hollow site off bewCloud's silent mock DB client.
